title: 36 Kế Trong Kinh Doanh Hiện Đại
author: Lan Bercu
summary:
36 Kế Trong Kinh Doanh Hiện Đại, published by NXB Trẻ (translated by Nguyễn Minh Phương, 2016), is Lan Bercu's application of the classical Chinese Thirty-Six Stratagems to modern business practice. Unlike a more purely historical or philosophical treatment of the stratagems, Bercu's book is explicitly structured as a practical business tool: each of the 36 stratagems is organized around a short, condensed Chinese historical anecdote, followed by relevant modern business situations where the underlying pattern applies, and concrete tools for putting the idea into practice.

A defining structural feature, confirmed across multiple bookseller descriptions, is that each stratagem's presentation closes with a set of reflection questions, designed to help the reader work out how to apply the underlying idea most appropriately to their own specific business situation, rather than simply presenting the stratagem as a fixed formula to copy. This reflects Bercu's stated aim, per publisher material, of organizing insight from many sources into a practical, concise structure that produces immediately usable lessons rather than abstract historical commentary.

The book's overall pitch, again per publisher framing, is that it helps readers unlock more creative and superior thinking in business by exposing them to strategies and tactics that fall outside conventional, orthodox business-school approaches — positioning the ancient stratagems as a source of flexible, adaptable thinking specifically because they were not originally designed for the business context they're now being applied to, and therefore require genuine interpretive work rather than direct copying.

Because this book's individual entries were not fully enumerated in available secondary sources beyond its overall structure and stated purpose, and because the underlying Thirty-Six Stratagems are well-established and independently verifiable as a classical text, this entry's section breakdown groups the 36 stratagems into broad category clusters based on the well-documented traditional groupings of the classical system (stratagems for when in a superior position, for confronting an enemy, for attack, for confused situations, for gaining ground, and for desperate situations), while relying on Bercu's confirmed structural format — anecdote, business application, tools, reflection questions — for how each entry within those clusters is presented.

sections.title: Stratagems for a Position of Strength
sections.summary:
This cluster covers stratagems traditionally applied when a company or negotiator holds a position of relative strength or advantage, focused on how to consolidate and extend that advantage without overreaching. Each entry follows Bercu's format: a short historical anecdote illustrating the classical stratagem, followed by a modern business scenario, practical tools, and closing reflection questions for the reader's own situation.

The section emphasizes that even from a position of strength, sustainable advantage requires deliberate strategy rather than passive reliance on an existing lead — recurring modern business applications include market leadership defense, negotiating from a position of leverage, and managing competitive complacency.

It transitions into the following cluster by noting that strength is rarely permanent in competitive markets, setting up the book's later material on how to act when facing a stronger competitor.
keyLessons: Actively manage and extend a competitive advantage rather than assuming it will persist passively.
Use a position of strength to negotiate deliberately rather than coasting on existing leverage.
Guard against complacency that a position of strength can create within an organization.

sections.title: Stratagems for Confronting a Stronger Opponent
sections.summary:
This cluster addresses situations where a business or negotiator faces a stronger, better-resourced competitor, focusing on indirect, asymmetric tactics rather than direct confrontation. Following the book's consistent format, each entry pairs a historical anecdote of an underdog outmaneuvering a stronger force with a modern business parallel — such as a smaller company using agility or niche focus to compete against a larger incumbent.

The reflection questions closing each entry in this section are aimed specifically at helping readers assess their own relative competitive position honestly, since Bercu's framework depends on correctly identifying whether you are the stronger or weaker party in a given situation before selecting an appropriate stratagem.

This cluster leads into the book's material on attack and initiative by establishing that even a weaker competitor has legitimate strategic options, provided they choose tactics matched to their actual position rather than imitating a stronger rival's direct approach.
keyLessons: Choose asymmetric, indirect tactics when facing a stronger competitor rather than imitating their direct approach.
Honestly assess your actual competitive position before selecting a strategic response.
Use agility and niche focus as legitimate competitive advantages against larger, slower incumbents.

sections.title: Stratagems for Attack and Initiative
sections.summary:
This cluster covers stratagems oriented toward proactively creating opportunity — timing an entry into a new market, seizing on a competitor's momentary weakness, or creating advantageous conditions rather than simply reacting to them. As with the other clusters, each entry follows the book's format of historical anecdote, business application, practical tools, and reflection questions.

The section emphasizes timing as a central theme — several of the classical stratagems in this category concern acting at the precise moment an opportunity is available, rather than either acting too early or waiting too long.

It transitions into the book's material on navigating uncertainty by noting that not every business situation offers a clear opportunity to seize, setting up the following cluster's focus on ambiguous or confused conditions.
keyLessons: Time proactive moves (market entry, competitive positioning) to specific windows of opportunity rather than acting on a fixed schedule.
Look for a competitor's moments of weakness or distraction as opportunities to gain ground.
Distinguish between genuine opportunities to seize and situations that merely resemble one.

sections.title: Stratagems for Uncertain and Desperate Situations
sections.summary:
This closing cluster addresses how to navigate ambiguous, chaotic, or genuinely difficult business situations, including scenarios resembling crisis or near-failure. Following the book's format, each entry pairs a historical anecdote of navigating extreme adversity with modern applications like crisis management, turnaround situations, and negotiating from a position of real weakness.

The reflection questions in this cluster are framed, per the book's consistent structure, to help readers assess not just tactical options but their own psychological readiness to act decisively under pressure, since Bercu's application of the stratagems treats mindset as inseparable from tactical choice in high-stakes situations.

The book closes without a single unifying case study, consistent with its stratagem-by-stratagem structure, ending instead on the reminder — implicit throughout the reflection-question format — that every stratagem requires deliberate adaptation to the reader's specific situation rather than direct, uncritical application.
keyLessons: Treat crisis and turnaround situations as requiring a distinct strategic toolkit, not simply an intensified version of normal-condition tactics.
Assess your own psychological readiness to act decisively under pressure as part of your strategic planning.
Adapt every stratagem in this book to your specific situation rather than applying it as a fixed formula.
Actively manage and extend a competitive advantage rather than assuming a strong position will persist on its own.
Choose asymmetric, indirect tactics when facing a stronger competitor rather than imitating their direct approach.
Honestly assess your actual competitive position before selecting a strategic response.
Time proactive competitive moves to specific windows of opportunity rather than a fixed schedule.
Look for a competitor's moments of weakness as opportunities to gain ground, without overreaching.
Treat crisis and turnaround situations as requiring a distinct strategic toolkit.
Use the book's closing reflection questions for every stratagem to adapt it to your specific business situation rather than copying it directly.
Draw on unconventional, non-business-school strategic thinking as a deliberate source of creative advantage.

conceptsFrameworks.name: Điển Tích Trung Hoa (Chinese Historical Anecdote) as Teaching Device
conceptsFrameworks.definition: Bercu's core structural device: each of the 36 stratagems opens with a condensed historical anecdote from Chinese history illustrating the underlying strategic logic, before the book translates that logic into a modern business application. The anecdote functions as a memorable, concrete anchor for an otherwise abstract strategic principle.

conceptsFrameworks.name: Reflection-Question Close
conceptsFrameworks.definition: Every stratagem entry in the book closes with a set of reflection questions designed to help the reader work out the most appropriate way to apply that stratagem's underlying idea to their own specific business situation, rather than presenting the stratagem as a fixed, one-size-fits-all formula.
conceptsFrameworks.sourceSection: Structural feature across all entries, explicitly confirmed in publisher description

actionSteps: Identify your business's current competitive position (strong, weak, or ambiguous) honestly, and select one stratagem category from this book that matches that position rather than one you find more appealing.
Apply one stratagem's reflection questions directly to a live business decision you're currently facing, and write out your answers before acting.
Identify one competitor's recent moment of visible weakness or distraction, and assess whether it represents a genuine window of opportunity for you.
Before your next high-stakes negotiation, explicitly plan for both an advantage scenario and a disadvantage scenario, using tactics appropriate to each.
reflectionQuestions: Which category of stratagem (strength, confronting a stronger rival, initiative, or crisis) best matches your business's current situation, and does your current strategy actually reflect that?
Where have you applied a "strong position" tactic while actually operating from a position of relative weakness, or vice versa?
What would change about your current strategic plan if you assumed your competitive advantage was temporary rather than durable?

points: Available secondary sources confirm the book's overall structure, format, and stated purpose but do not provide a full, verifiable enumeration of all 36 individual entries' modern business examples; this entry's section breakdown therefore relies on the well-documented traditional categorization of the classical Thirty-Six Stratagems rather than a confirmed chapter-by-chapter reading of Bercu's specific text, and should be understood as a reasonable structural approximation rather than a verified table of contents.

As with any modern business application of a centuries-old military and political text, the mapping from historical anecdote (often involving warfare, court intrigue, or life-and-death political maneuvering) to a modern competitive business situation necessarily involves significant interpretive license, and readers should treat the parallels as illustrative and thought-provoking rather than as rigorously validated business strategy research.

The book's promotional framing emphasizes unconventional, non-business-school thinking as an advantage, but this framing is not independently substantiated with comparative evidence against conventional strategic frameworks; readers should treat it as the author's stated philosophy rather than an evaluated claim.
criticalTake.contextNote: Not applicable — insufficient independently verifiable detail on specific entry content to assess how individual claims in this edition have aged.

whoThisIsFor: Business owners and managers interested in creative, unconventional strategic thinking drawn from classical Chinese stratagem, particularly those who want a structured self-reflection exercise (via the book's closing questions) rather than a purely prescriptive playbook.
whenToReadThis: Useful when facing a specific competitive or negotiation challenge and looking for a fresh strategic frame outside conventional business-school approaches, using the relevant stratagem's reflection questions as a structured planning exercise.

authorBio.name: Lan Bercu
authorBio.bio:
Lan Bercu is the author of 36 Kế Trong Kinh Doanh Hiện Đại, published in Vietnamese by NXB Trẻ (translated by Nguyễn Minh Phương) with an English-language original edition also available under the same title's transliterated form. Bercu appeared in person to discuss the book with readers at a public event at NXB Trẻ's bookstall on Đường Sách Nguyễn Văn Bình in Ho Chi Minh City, drawing interest from readers, businesspeople, and aspiring entrepreneurs.

Beyond the book's own publisher materials and this public event, limited independently verifiable biographical detail about the author was found in available sources.

The section-level grouping into strength/weakness/initiative/crisis categories follows the well-documented traditional structure of the classical Thirty-Six Stratagems rather than a confirmed reading of this specific book's internal table of contents, which was not available in full; this is flagged explicitly as an approximation rather than presented as verified original chapter content.
